    5.1Examplespp. 83–86

    Four model problems. Three are linear (X-ray tomography, kriging with linear , the backward heat equation); the elliptic coefficient problem is the nonlinear model problem used for the rest of the chapter.

    For the examNot on the topics list. The list numbers this chapter one lower than the draft, so its 5.1 is Section 5.2 here, and the examples section has no counterpart. Keep it as context: the heat-equation picture is a quick way to explain ill-posedness and why the prior dominates high modes.

    X-ray tomography. Beer–Lambert attenuation integrates to (5.1.1): . Data along lines give with the Radon transform, compact, so the inverse is unbounded. Bayesian version: , , target .

    Kriging / Gaussian process regression. , concatenated as . With Gaussian prior and noise this is Example 4.3.9:

    The exponent is the data misfit potential. For linear the posterior is Gaussian (Thm 5.3.1): that is GP regression.

    Backward heat equation. . In sine coefficients the problem is diagonal:

    Inverting multiplies the noise in mode by : exponential ill-posedness.

    Elliptic coefficient problem. Recover in from . Even with linear, is nonlinear, so is nonlinear. This problem drives Sections 5.2, 5.4, 5.5 and 5.6.

    Intuition

    Ill-posedness is a statement about how fast the singular values of the forward map decay. Radon: polynomially (mildly ill-posed, order 1/2 in 2D). Heat: like (severely ill-posed). In the Bayesian picture this decides how many modes the data can inform: mode is informed only while ( = prior standard deviation, = noise level). For the heat equation that cutoff grows only like , so reducing noise by orders of magnitude buys one or two extra modes. The demo below shows this.

    Edge cases & traps
    • The heat problem is written with and additive noise on all coefficients. Independent noise on infinitely many coefficients is white noise: it is not in , let alone . Either the noise is coloured (trace-class covariance) or the data are truncated to finitely many coefficients. Section 5.2 takes the second route (truncation after terms).
    • "The inverse Radon transform involves differentiating the data": that is the source of instability for complete data. Limited-angle data are worse: some features are invisible (nontrivial kernel), which the prior must fill in.

    5.2Discretisationpp. 86–90

    Discretising the forward model perturbs the posterior. The question of this section: if the forward solver has error in the observed functional, is the posterior also away, and in which metric? Answer: yes, in Hellinger distance, via the stability Theorem 4.4.1.

    For the examTopics list 5.1: idea and consequence of FEM; its Thm 5.1.6 is Thm 5.2.6 here and is the one singled out: how influences the posterior. Know the chain: FE rates (energy) and (functionals) → Thm 4.4.1 gives → Lemma 3.7.7 gives for posterior expectations. Lax–Milgram and regularity details are background.

    Theorem 5.2.6FE error in the posteriorCorep. 89–90

    Assume and the assumptions of Thm 5.2.5 with . Let be bounded linear, , , with posteriors and under the noise model (5.2.2). Then

    For any bounded linear , , :

    PROOF STRUCTURE
    1. Hellinger: Thm 4.4.1 with the same data and , gives , and (5.2.6) with makes the last factor .
    2. Moment transfer (5.2.9): the Gaussian likelihood is , so . Posterior moments are controlled by prior moments.
    3. Split (5.2.10): . First term: (5.2.9) + (5.2.6) with . Second: Lemma 3.7.7, , and the moments are finite by (5.2.9) + Thm 5.2.1.
    Intuition

    Two ingredients. (i) Theorem 4.4.1 says the posterior is Lipschitz in the forward map, measured in , i.e. averaged over the prior. So the posterior inherits the forward rate in the mean-square sense, which is exactly what Thm 5.2.5 provides. (ii) Hellinger controls expectations of square-integrable functions (Lemma 3.7.7), so a Hellinger rate becomes a rate for posterior means. Note the order of logic: this is a bias statement. It says nothing about sampling error, which is Sections 5.4 to 5.6.

    Edge cases & traps
    • The constant is not noise-robust. and as or . A concentrated posterior needs a finer mesh for the same bias. The demo below shows the curve shifting up as decreases.
    • The bound uses , an average over the prior. A mesh that is accurate where the posterior lives but poor elsewhere is still penalised; the constant can be pessimistic.
    • Hellinger is a metric, so the prior truncation error (Rem. 5.2.7(b)) adds: . Balance when choosing .

    5.3Linear problems and the Laplace approximationpp. 90–93

    Linear forward map, Gaussian prior, additive Gaussian noise: the posterior is Gaussian and explicit. For everything else, the Laplace approximation fits a Gaussian at the MAP point; it becomes exact in the small-noise limit at rate in Hellinger.

    For the examTopics list 5.2: examined in full.
    Theorem 5.3.1linear-Gaussian posteriorCorep. 91

    Let be separable Hilbert, with positive covariance operator , on independent of , SPD, and with linear. Then with

    PROOF IDEA () is jointly Gaussian (5.3.3) with covariance , using . Block elimination with (SPD, hence invertible) diagonalises it; the Schur complement is . The quadratic form splits as , and the conditional density is proportional to the first factor: completing the square.
    Intuition
    • Precision form (finite dimensions, via Woodbury): and . Information adds. The notes' form (5.3.1)–(5.3.2) inverts an matrix (cheap when data are few) and makes sense in infinite dimensions, where is unbounded.
    • does not depend on , and : data can only reduce uncertainty in the linear-Gaussian case.
    • : generalised Tikhonov (Sect. 2.6) with the Cameron–Martin norm as penalty. The Kalman update (5.8.6) is literally this theorem.
    Edge cases & traps
    • In infinite dimensions the Cameron–Martin space has prior measure zero, so "" is infinite for prior samples. The MAP characterisation still holds as a minimiser over the Cameron–Martin space.
    • From (5.3.2), . So a direction keeps its full prior variance iff . Having is not enough: the prior can correlate an unobserved direction with an observed one, and then data on the latter shrink the former.
    Definition 5.3.2Laplace approximation (Laplace, 1774)Corep. 92

    Let and prior density be on . Set

    and assume has a unique minimiser with and SPD. The Laplace approximation is

    Intuition

    Second-order Taylor expansion of the negative log posterior at its minimiser. With : . Dropping the middle term (residual times curvature) gives the Gauss–Newton Hessian, which is always positive semidefinite and is what codes often use. For linear and Gaussian prior, Laplace is exact and equals Thm 5.3.1. Computing : quasi-Newton (BFGS, SR1) with line search or trust region.

    Edge cases & traps
    • Multimodal posterior. Example 5.6.16 (, ) has two symmetric modes; "unique minimiser" fails and any Laplace approximation sits on one mode, keeping half the mass away. Hellinger distance does not go to zero. Demo option 2.
    • Degenerate Hessian. If at the limit point, the data-misfit Hessian vanishes. Example: , , prior , noise variance : for every , so the Laplace approximation is the prior , while the posterior has width . Demo option 3: .
    • Not invariant under reparametrisation: the MAP of is not the log of the MAP of (the Jacobian enters the density).

    Self-test
    Show that x_CM = x_MAP in the linear-Gaussian case.
    The posterior density is , a Gaussian, whose mean and mode coincide. Equivalently the MAP objective is a strictly convex quadratic whose minimiser solves , which is by Woodbury.
    Why is the Laplace approximation useful as an importance distribution or MCMC proposal, even when it is not accurate?
    It captures the scale and orientation of the posterior (Hessian at the mode), so a sampler preconditioned with it is robust in the small-noise limit: (5.5.9), Thm 5.5.11. The prior, in contrast, puts a vanishing fraction of samples where the posterior lives.
    State the hypotheses of Definition 5.3.2 and give one violation for each.
    Unique minimiser: violated by , (two modes). Stationarity with SPD Hessian: violated by , in the limit (Hessian of the misfit is 0). regularity: violated by a Laplace (double-exponential) prior at 0.

    5.6The Markov chain Monte Carlo methodpp. 110–123

    Build a Markov chain whose invariant measure is the posterior, run it, average along the path. Detailed balance gives invariance for free; ergodicity gives convergence; the autocorrelation decides the price per effective sample. The infinite-dimensional view explains why random walk proposals degrade with the discretisation and pCN does not.

    For the examTopics list 5.5: examined, except Section 5.6.4 on more efficient proposal kernels (the list calls it 5.5.4).

    5.6.4More efficient proposals and multilevel MCMCpp. 122–123

    • Adaptive: DRAM (Haario et al.) learns the RW covariance and adds delayed rejection.
    • Gradient: the deterministic move converges to a mode and stops exploring. MALA proposes , one Euler–Maruyama step of the Langevin SDE , whose invariant density is ; tune to .
    • Hamiltonian: HMC (Duane et al. 1987), NUTS (Hoffman–Gelman 2014).
    • Hessian information: RMHMC (Girolami–Calderhead), DILI (Cui–Law–Marzouk), gpCN (Rudolf–Sprungk).
    • Surrogate transition / delayed acceptance (Liu; Christen–Fox): stage 1 is MH for a cheap surrogate with ; stage 2 accepts with
      The expensive is evaluated only for stage-1 survivors. With a coarse-mesh posterior this leads to multilevel MCMC (Dodwell et al. 2019; Lykkegaard et al. 2023).

    5.7Variational methodspp. 124–132

    Replace sampling by optimisation: pick the member of a tractable family closest to the posterior in reverse KL. The ELBO removes the unknown evidence. Mean-field gives closed-form coordinate updates but no correlations; transport maps make the family as rich as you can parametrise, and triangular maps turn joint samplers into conditional (posterior) samplers.

    For the examTopics list 5.6: only the idea that it is optimisation, and how these methods compare with the rest of the lecture. No details, equations or results. What to be able to say:
    • VI picks the best approximation to the posterior within a chosen tractable family (Gaussians, product measures, pushforwards by a map class), measured in KL: inference becomes an optimisation problem.
    • Sampling methods (MC, ratio estimators, MCMC; 5.4–5.6) are asymptotically exact: more samples, smaller error. VI has a bias set by the family that more compute does not remove; in exchange it is fast, scales with gradient methods, and the result is cheap to evaluate and sample.
    • Closest relative in the lecture: the Laplace approximation (5.3), also a Gaussian surrogate but built from mode and curvature. Both can precondition sampling methods (5.5.3).
    • Typical failure: the KL used in VI is mode-seeking, so uncertainty is underestimated and modes can be missed (demo below). Transport maps make the family rich enough to be exact in principle.

    Problem (5.7.1): , a variational family of tractable measures (e.g. i.i.d. sampling is easy). Existence and uniqueness depend on . Finite dimensions: , (5.7.2).

    • The map depends on the ordering of the variables; different orderings give different KR maps. It is generally not the optimal transport (Brenier) map; it arises as a limit of optimal transport with increasingly anisotropic quadratic costs (Carlier, Galichon, Santambrogio).

    5.8Sequential Monte Carlo methods & Bayesian filteringpp. 132–140

    Data arrive in time. Filtering alternates a prediction (push the current distribution through the dynamics) with a Bayes update (Thm 5.3.1 in the linear-Gaussian case). The Kalman filter is exact there; EKF linearises; EnKF replaces the covariance by an ensemble; particle filters replace the Gaussian update by importance weights.

    For the examTopics list 5.7: idea of Bayesian filtering and how it relates to the rest. No details, equations or results; no SMC. What to be able to say:
    • The unknown is a state that evolves in time and data arrive sequentially. Filtering alternates prediction (push the current posterior through the dynamics; this becomes the next prior) and a Bayes update with the new datum.
    • So filtering is a sequence of Bayesian inverse problems solved recursively, with a fixed cost per step and no need to revisit old data. The earlier chapters solve one static problem.
    • Linear-Gaussian case: every update is Thm 5.3.1, which is the Kalman filter. Nonlinear variants approximate: linearisation (EKF), an ensemble for the covariance (EnKF), importance weights (particle filters).
    • Vocabulary worth knowing: prediction, filtering and smoothing distributions (Def 5.8.2).

    If is SPD then every from (5.8.6) is symmetric positive definite.

    PROOF (the exercise) Induction. is SPD since is. Woodbury: , the inverse of an SPD matrix.
    Edge cases & traps
    • The covariance recursion does not involve the data: can be precomputed and converges (under observability/controllability) to the solution of a discrete algebraic Riccati equation.
    • In floating point, can lose symmetry and positivity. The Joseph form is algebraically equal and numerically safe.
    • Cost: storing and propagating covariances, per step. For weather models () impossible, which motivates EnKF.

    5.8.3Extended Kalman filterpp. 136–137

    Nonlinear , linear . Linearise at the current mean: , . Predict , ; update as in (5.8.6).

    Edge cases & traps
    • The mean is propagated exactly through , the covariance only through its linearisation. If the uncertainty is large relative to the curvature of , the predicted covariance is wrong and the filter can diverge (become overconfident and ignore the data).
    • Always Gaussian: a filtering distribution that becomes bimodal (e.g. a double-well system observed sparsely) cannot be represented. Demo below.

    Intuition
    • Why perturb the observations: with the unperturbed update all members move by and the analysis spread is , too small. Adding adds in expectation, which gives the Joseph form, i.e. the correct Kalman covariance for linear models.
    • Linear-Gaussian: EnKF KF as .
    Edge cases & traps
    • Not a consistent filter for nonlinear models. As the EnKF converges to a mean-field limit (Le Gland, Monbet, Tran 2011) that differs from the true filtering distribution unless the model is linear-Gaussian. It is a Gaussian-type update applied to non-Gaussian ensembles.
    • The update keeps particles in the span of the forecast anomalies: rank . With , sampling noise creates spurious long-range correlations; practice uses localisation and covariance inflation.

    Check against the notes
    • The observation model is printed as ; consistent with (5.8.2) and the weights, it should be .
    • In the Bayes formulas the denominator integrates against (resp. written next to ); it should be the predictive distribution, the same measure as in the numerator. The last display's left side should read .
    Edge cases & traps
    • Weight degeneracy. Without resampling the weights are a product of likelihoods over time; their variance grows (typically exponentially) and after a few steps one particle carries all the weight. Remedy: resample (multinomial, systematic) when drops below, say, (bootstrap / SIR filter). The notes only mention this in the final sentence; it is the difference between a working and a useless particle filter.
    • Dimension. For a fixed error, the required grows exponentially with the effective dimension of the observations (Bengtsson, Bickel, Li 2008; Snyder et al.). This is the same mechanism as Lemma 5.5.10: prior-as-proposal importance sampling against a concentrated likelihood.
    • Consistency () holds for nonlinear, non-Gaussian models, unlike EKF and EnKF.

    Which of KF, EKF, EnKF, PF are exact / consistent, and under what conditions?
    KF: exact for linear-Gaussian. EKF: approximate always (exact only when linear). EnKF: consistent as only in the linear-Gaussian case. PF: consistent as for general models (with resampling for stable constants over time).
    How does the particle filter weight update relate to Section 5.5?
